title: The Morning Snow Report
text:
Good morning! This is Weather Wendy with your snow report. Last night, our town got {number} inches of fresh snow. The snow is very {adjective} today, which is perfect for sled rides.

It is cold outside, so please wear your coat, your hat, and two pairs of {plural noun}. Watch out for slippery {plural noun} on the sidewalk. The wind is blowing {adverb} from the north, and it smells a little bit like {food}.

This afternoon, we expect clouds shaped like {plural noun} and snowflakes the size of a {noun}. Kids may want to {verb} in the front yard before lunch. Grown-ups should shovel the driveway and the {noun}.

Tonight, the moon will be big and {adjective}. Please drink something warm and say goodnight to your {adjective} snowman. This has been Weather Wendy. Stay warm and keep {verb ending in ing}!

title: A Message from Principal Plum
text:
Good morning, families. This is Principal Plum. Because of all the snow, school is closed today. The parking lot is covered in snow up to my {body part}, and the buses are stuck behind a giant pile of {plural noun}. I am at home right now, {verb ending in ing} in my pajamas.

Do not worry about our class gerbil, Peanut. Mr. Diaz went in early to feed him three {plural noun} and give him a tiny {adjective} blanket. Peanut {past tense verb} to say thank you.

Please use this day to read a book, drink warm cocoa, and {verb} with your family. If you build a snowman, bring a picture to class. The most {adjective} snowman will win a {noun} for the whole class. Snowmen with {adjective} hats get extra points.

Stay safe, stay warm, and please wear your {color} mittens. Tomorrow, please walk into school {adverb} and stomp the snow off your {plural noun}.

title: How to Build the Best Snowman
text:
Building a snowman is easy if you follow these steps. Ask a {adjective} grown-up to help with the heavy parts.

First, roll a big ball of snow for the bottom. Keep rolling until it is as big as a {noun}. Then make a middle ball and a small {adjective} head. Stack them up {adverb} so they do not fall over. Pat the snow smooth with your {body part}.

Next, give your snowman a face. Use two {plural noun} for the eyes and a carrot for the nose. For the mouth, make a smile out of little {plural noun}. If you do not have any, you can use {food} instead.

Last, dress him up. Wrap a {color} scarf around his neck and put an old {noun} on his head. Give him two sticks for arms so he can {verb} at the cars going by. Now step back and look. He is so {adjective}! If you listen closely, you might hear him {verb ending in ing}.

title: Grandpa's Snow Day Cocoa
text:
On every snow day, Grandpa makes his famous hot cocoa. Here is his recipe.

First, pour two cups of milk into a pot. Grandpa says to stir it {adverb}, or the milk gets {adjective}. Then add three spoonfuls of cocoa powder and one tiny pinch of {plural noun}. That is his secret.

While it warms up, Grandpa likes to {verb} around the kitchen and hum a song about {plural noun}. He says it makes the cocoa taste {adjective}. Our cat, Pepper, sits on a {noun} and watches him {verb ending in ing}.

When the cocoa is warm, pour it into your favorite mug. Add {number} marshmallows, plus a {noun} if you are feeling fancy. Drink it slowly while you look out at the {adjective} snow. After the first sip, Grandpa always closes his eyes and says, "{exclamation}! That tastes like {food}!"

title: My Snow Day Diary
text:
Dear Diary,
When I woke up today, everything outside was white! School was closed. I was so happy that I {past tense verb} all the way down the stairs.

After breakfast, my brother and I put on our snow pants, boots, and {plural noun}. It took us {number} minutes. By the time we got outside, I was already a little bit {adjective}.

First we made snow angels. Mine looked like a {adjective} {animal}. Then we had a snowball contest with our {adjective} neighbor, Mrs. Kim. She throws very {adverb}. Our dog, Muffin, was {verb ending in ing} in the yard. Then he jumped into a snow pile and came out looking like a {noun}.

Now I am inside, drinking cocoa and watching the snow fall {adverb}. My cheeks are pink, and my toes feel like {plural noun}. I hope tomorrow is a snow day too, so I can {verb} all over again.

title: The Great Sled Race Results
text:
Here are the official results of the Great Sled Race on Maple Hill. The judges were Mr. Lopez and his {adjective} cat. Mr. Lopez kept time with a {noun}.

In third place is Sam. Sam rode a red sled and shouted, "{exclamation}!" the whole way down. He wins a cup of cocoa and a {adjective} sticker.

In second place is Priya. She rode down the hill on a {noun} and finished in {number} seconds. The judges say she was very {adjective}. She wins a pair of fuzzy {plural noun}.

In first place is Grandma Bea! She rode her old wooden sled and went down {adverb}. At the bottom, she {past tense verb} and waved her {plural noun} at the crowd. She wins the golden trophy and a bag of {plural noun}. Next year, everyone wants to {verb} like Grandma Bea.

title: Rules for Our Snow Fort
text:
My friends and I built a snow fort in my backyard. It has two rooms, a window, and a flag made from a {color} sock. Here are our rules.

Rule one: Say the secret word before coming in. This week, the secret word is "{silly word}." Rule two: No more than {number} kids inside at once, or the walls start to wiggle.

Rule three: Please do not {verb} inside the fort. Last time, Theo did that, and the roof dripped on his {noun}. He {past tense verb} for an hour. Rule four: Snacks are allowed, but only crackers and {plural noun}. Crumbs make the floor {adjective}.

Rule five: Wipe your {plural noun} on the mat. Rule six: Be nice to our guard, a {adjective} snowman who is always {verb ending in ing}. Rule seven: When it is time to go inside, say goodbye to the fort {adverb}. Our fort is the most {adjective} place in the whole neighborhood!

title: Dear Snow, Please Come Back
text:
Dear Snow,
Thank you for coming to our town last week. You were very {adjective}, and you covered everything, even our mailbox and Dad's {noun}. We had the best time. Even the squirrels were {verb ending in ing}.

My sister and I made a snowman named Mr. Pebble. He had two {plural noun} for eyes and a big {adjective} smile. We also made {number} snow angels in a row. Mom hung a picture of them on the {noun}.

Now you have melted, and the yard is just mud and {plural noun}. Mr. Pebble's scarf is still lying in the grass. I {past tense verb} a little when I saw it.

Please come back soon. If you do, I promise to {verb} with you all day and wear my {adjective} mittens. I will even leave a bowl of {food} on the porch for you. Please write back {adverb}.
Love,
Owen

title: How to Get Ready for the Snow
text:
Going out in the snow takes a lot of work. Mom wrote this list on the back of a {noun} so I do not forget anything.

First, put on your warmest shirt and your {adjective} socks. Then pull on your snow pants. You may need to {verb} to get them all the way up. They make a {adjective} sound when you walk. Next, zip your coat all the way up to your {body part}.

Now it is time for boots. Push your feet in {adverb}. If they will not go in, check for {plural noun} hiding inside. Last time, I found my brother's {noun} in there. Then put on your hat, your scarf, and your {plural noun}. By now you will look like a big {adjective} {noun}.

Last of all, open the door and step outside. Take two steps in the snow and start {verb ending in ing}. Then Mom will knock on the window and say it is time to come in for {food}.

title: A Snowman Tells All
text:
Today our school newspaper talked to Frosty Fred, the snowman who stands {adverb} in front of the library.

We asked Fred how he feels about snow days. "I love them," he said. "Kids give me {plural noun} and a new {noun} to wear. Yesterday, a girl named Kaya gave me a hug so {adjective} that I almost lost my nose. My arms are just sticks, but I am very good at {verb ending in ing}."

We asked Fred what he does at night. "Mostly I stand here," he said {adverb}. "Sometimes I watch the {plural noun} go by. When nobody is looking, I like to {verb} a little. Last night, I {past tense verb} until the sun came up."

We asked Fred for advice. "Always wear {adjective} mittens," he said. "Eat a warm bowl of {food} after playing outside. And please, never let the {animal} near my carrot nose." Thank you, Fred. Stay {adjective}!
